q2_1_0_0:
Classification of Opioid Analgesics & Morphine

Classification

Natural: Morphine, Codeine, Papaverine, Noscapine. Semisynthetic: Heroin, Hydrocodone, Oxycodone, Hydromorphone, Buprenorphine. Synthetic: Pethidine, Fentanyl, Methadone, Tramadol, Tapentadol, Dextropropoxyphene. Antagonists: Naloxone, Naltrexone. Mixed: Pentazocine, Butorphanol, Nalbuphine.

Pharmacological Actions of Morphine

CNS: Analgesia (mu & kappa receptors); sedation; euphoria; respiratory depression (↓ CO2 response); miosis (no tolerance); nausea/vomiting (CTZ). GI: Constipation (↑ sphincter tone, ↓ peristalsis); biliary spasm. CV: Vasodilation (histamine); hypotension; bradycardia; ↑ ICP. GU: Urinary retention; ↑ ADH. Skin: Flushing, pruritus (histamine).

Therapeutic Uses

Moderate-severe pain (post-op, MI, cancer, trauma); acute pulmonary oedema (venodilation, anxiolysis); anaesthesia adjunct (fentanyl); cough (codeine); diarrhoea (loperamide); opioid substitution (methadone, buprenorphine).

Adverse Effects

Respiratory depression (most dangerous); constipation (universal, no tolerance); nausea; sedation; pruritus; urinary retention; tolerance (to analgesia, euphoria, respiratory depression — NOT constipation/miosis); dependence (physical withdrawal + psychological craving). Overdose triad: coma + pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression → naloxone 0.4-2 mg IV/IM.

Contraindications

Respiratory depression, severe asthma/COPD; raised ICP; intestinal obstruction; biliary colic (use pethidine); head injury; MAOI therapy (serotonin syndrome — pethidine, tramadol).

Clinical Pearl

WHO analgesic ladder: Step 1 (non-opioid ± adjuvant) → Step 2 (weak opioid ± non-opioid ± adjuvant) → Step 3 (strong opioid ± non-opioid ± adjuvant). Always co-prescribe laxative with opioids — constipation universal. Naloxone is antidote for overdose. Fentanyl — transdermal for chronic cancer pain; 100× more potent than morphine. Methadone — opioid substitution; long-acting. Buprenorphine — partial agonist; ceiling on respiratory depression. India — opioid access severely restricted (NDPS Act); morphine consumption among lowest globally despite high cancer burden.
q2_1_0_1:
Anti-tubercular Drugs

Classification

First-line: Isoniazid (H), Rifampicin (R), Pyrazinamide (Z), Ethambutol (E). Second-line injectable: Amikacin, Kanamycin, Capreomycin, Streptomycin. Fluoroquinolones: Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin. Group D1: Ethionamide, Cycloserine, Linezolid, Clofazimine. Group D2: Bedaquiline, Delamanid.

First-Line Mechanism, Uses, Adverse Effects

Isoniazid (H): Inhibits mycolic acid synthesis (inhA); bactericidal; penetrates CSF. Uses: all TB, latent TB. ADR: peripheral neuropathy (give pyridoxine B6 10-25 mg/day); hepatotoxicity; drug-induced lupus. Acetylated by NAT2 (slow vs fast acetylators).

Rifampicin (R): Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (rpoB); bactericidal; sterilising action (kills dormant bacilli). Uses: all TB, leprosy, meningococcal prophylaxis. ADR: hepatotoxicity; orange urine/sweat/tears; flu-like syndrome; potent CYP inducer (↓ warfarin, OCPs, steroids, PIs, ketoconazole, digoxin, ciclosporin).

Pyrazinamide (Z): Converted to pyrazinoic acid; disrupts membrane energy; bactericidal in acidic environment (macrophages); sterilising. Uses: intensive phase only (2 months). ADR: hepatotoxicity (most hepatotoxic); hyperuricaemia (gout); arthralgia.

Ethambutol (E): Inhibits arabinosyl transferase (embB); bacteriostatic; prevents resistance. Uses: intensive phase. ADR: optic neuritis (↓ visual acuity, red-green colour blindness; monitor vision monthly; reversible if caught early); hyperuricaemia.

NTEP Regimen

Drug-sensitive TB: HRZE × 2 months intensive + HRE × 4 months continuation = 6 months. MDR-TB: BPaL (Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid) × 6 months.

Clinical Pearl

Always give pyridoxine (B6) with isoniazid (prevents neuropathy). Monitor LFT (H+R+Z hepatotoxicity). Monitor vision with ethambutol. Rifampicin — potent CYP inducer (check ALL medications). Orange urine normal. MDR-TB — BPaL regimen (6 months) revolutionary. India NTEP — free diagnosis & treatment; daily therapy; CBNAAT for diagnosis & rifampicin resistance.
q2_1_0_2:
Classification of Anti-epileptic Drugs

Classification by Mechanism

Na+ channel blockers (use-dependent): Phenytoin, Carbamazepine, Lamotrigine, Oxcarbazepine, Eslicarbazepine, Lacosamide, Rufinamide, Topiramate, Zonisamide, Valproate.

Calcium channel blockers: Ethosuximide (T-type, absence seizures); Gabapentin, Pregabalin (alpha-2-delta subunit); Verapamil (investigational for cluster headache).

GABA enhancers: Benzodiazepines (Diazepam, Lorazepam, Clonazepam, Clobazam); Barbiturates (Phenobarbital, Primidone); Vigabatrin (irreversible GABA-T inhibitor); Tiagabine (GAT-1 inhibitor).

Glutamate antagonists: Perampanel (AMPA antagonist); Felbamate (NMDA antagonist — restricted use, aplastic anaemia risk).

SV2A ligands: Levetiracetam, Brivaracetam.

Broad-spectrum: Valproate, Lamotrigine, Topiramate, Levetiracetam, Zonisamide, Felbamate, Rufinamide.

Narrow-spectrum (focal): Phenytoin, Carbamazepine, Oxcarbazepine, Gabapentin, Pregabalin, Lacosamide, Eslicarbazepine.

Phenytoin — Mechanism, Uses, Adverse Effects

Mechanism: Use-dependent blockade of voltage-gated Na+ channels → ↓ sustained high-frequency repetitive firing → ↓ seizure spread. Zero-order kinetics (saturation at therapeutic doses; small dose changes → large level changes).

Uses: Focal (partial) seizures; generalized tonic-clonic; status epilepticus (IV fosphenytoin); trigeminal neuralgia; cardiac arrhythmias (class Ib antiarrhythmic).

Adverse effects: Gum hypertrophy (↑ collagen synthesis — dental hygiene); hirsutism; coarse facial features; acne; osteomalacia (↑ vitamin D metabolism — CYP inducer); megaloblastic anaemia (↓ folate absorption); neuropathy; nystagmus, ataxia, confusion (dose-related CNS toxicity); zero-order kinetics → narrow therapeutic index (10-20 µg/mL); drug interactions (CYP inducer — ↓ OCPs, warfarin, corticosteroids, cyclosporine, doxycycline, theophylline; CYP inhibitors ↑ phenytoin — isoniazid, sulphonamides, chloramphenicol, cimetidine, fluconazole, amiodarone, diltiazem, fluoxetine, omeprazole). Contraindications: absence seizures (may worsen), pregnancy (teratogenic — fetal hydantoin syndrome: cleft lip/palate, cardiac defects, nail/digit hypoplasia, growth retardation).

Clinical Pearl

Phenytoin has zero-order (saturable) kinetics — small dose increases cause disproportionately large plasma level increases → toxicity. Always monitor levels (10-20 µg/mL). Gum hypertrophy — encourage dental hygiene. CYP inducer — many drug interactions. Teratogenic — avoid in pregnancy (use levetiracetam, lamotrigine). Newer AEDs preferred: levetiracetam (no interactions, no hepatic metabolism, broad-spectrum), lamotrigine (mood stabilizer too, broad-spectrum), topiramate (migraine prophylaxis, weight loss).
q2_1_0_3:
Hormonal Contraceptives

Types

Combined oral contraceptives (COCs): Estrogen (ethinylestradiol) + Progestin (levonorgestrel, norethisterone, drospirenone, desogestrel). Progestin-only pills (POPs/mini-pills): Levonorgestrel, norethisterone, desogestrel. Injectable: DMPA (Depo-Provera) — every 3 months. Implants: Etonogestrel (Implanon NXT — 3 years), Levonorgestrel (Jadelle — 5 years). Transdermal patch: Norelgestromin/ethinylestradiol (Xulane — weekly). Vaginal ring: Etonogestrel/ethinylestradiol (NuvaRing — monthly). Emergency contraception: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg within 72h; ulipristal acetate 30 mg within 120h; copper IUD within 5 days. IUD: Levonorgestrel IUD (Mirena — 5-8 years); Copper IUD (ParaGard — 10 years).

Mechanism

COCs: (1) Suppress ovulation (↓ FSH, ↓ LH surge → no follicular development, no ovulation); (2) Thicken cervical mucus (↓ sperm penetration); (3) Thin endometrium (↓ implantation); (4) Alter tubal motility. POPs: mainly (2) and (3); ovulation suppression variable (more with desogestrel). DMPA: reliably suppresses ovulation.

Adverse Effects

Estrogen-related: Nausea, breast tenderness, fluid retention, headache, thrombosis (DVT, PE, stroke, MI — ↑ with smoking >35 yr); hypertension; melasma. Progestin-related: Weight gain, mood changes, acne (androgenic progestins — levonorgestrel; less with drospirenone — antiandrogenic); irregular bleeding/amenorrhoea. Serious: VTE (estrogen dose-dependent; 3-5× baseline risk; drospirenone slightly higher risk); stroke/MI (especially smokers >35); breast cancer (slight ↑ risk; disappears 10 years after stopping); cervical cancer (↑ with HPV); liver adenoma (rare).

Contraindications

Absolute: pregnancy; breastfeeding <6 weeks postpartum; smoking >15 cigarettes/day & age >35; hypertension (SBP >160 or DBP >100); VTE/PE (current or history); ischaemic heart disease; stroke; complicated valvular heart disease; migraine with aura (any age); breast cancer (current); liver disease (cirrhosis, hepatitis, tumour); diabetes with vascular complications; SLE with antiphospholipid; major surgery with prolonged immobilisation.

Non-contraceptive Benefits

↓ Ovarian cancer (50% ↓); ↓ endometrial cancer (50% ↓); ↓ colorectal cancer; regular cycles; ↓ dysmenorrhoea; ↓ menstrual blood loss; ↓ acne (with antiandrogenic progestins); ↓ premenstrual syndrome; treatment of endometriosis, PCOS, menorrhagia.

Clinical Pearl

WHO MEC (Medical Eligibility Criteria) guides contraceptive choice. Smokers >35 must NOT use estrogen-containing contraceptives — ↑ stroke/MI risk. POPs/DMPA/IUD safe in smokers, hypertension, migraine with aura (no estrogen). Drospirenone (antiandrogenic) — improves acne, hirsutism; but ↑ VTE risk. LNG-IUD (Mirena) — also treats menorrhagia, endometriosis, endometrial protection in estrogen therapy; 5-8 year duration. Emergency contraception — levonorgestrel 1.5 mg within 72h (most effective if taken ASAP); copper IUD within 5 days (most effective emergency contraception). India — family planning programme: free contraceptives (COCs, POPs, DMPA, condoms, IUDs); sterilization (tubectomy/vasectomy) — most common method; increasing use of IUDs & implants.

Drug Therapy of P. vivax Malaria

Treatment of P. vivax Malaria (NTEP/WHO Guidelines)

1. Chloroquine-sensitive P. vivax (most of India):

  • Chloroquine: 10 mg/kg on day 1 (600 mg base), then 10 mg/kg on day 2 (600 mg), then 5 mg/kg on day 3 (300 mg) — total 25 mg/kg over 3 days.
  • Primaquine: 0.25 mg/kg daily × 14 days (15 mg/day adult) — radical cure (kills hypnozoites in liver to prevent relapse). MUST check G6PD before giving primaquine.

2. Chloroquine-resistant P. vivax (northeast India, Indonesia, PNG):

  • ACT: Artemether-lumefantrine OR artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine × 3 days.
  • Plus Primaquine 0.25-0.5 mg/kg daily × 14 days.

3. Severe P. vivax malaria:

  • IV Artesunate: 2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12, 24 h, then daily until oral tolerated → ACT × 3 days + primaquine × 14 days.

Chloroquine — Mechanism, Adverse Effects

Mechanism: Concentrates in parasite food vacuole; inhibits haem polymerase → toxic haem accumulates → parasite death. Also raises vacuolar pH → inhibits protein degradation.

Adverse effects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea; headache; pruritus (especially dark-skinned — tolbutamide-responsive); skin rash; photosensitivity; bluish-black pigmentation; retinopathy (bull's eye maculopathy — with chronic high doses >5 years; hydroxychloroquine less toxic); ototoxicity; QT prolongation; hypoglycaemia; neuropsychiatric (rare — psychosis, seizures). Contraindications: psoriasis (may exacerbate); epilepsy; retinopathy; G6PD deficiency (haemolysis — relative).

Primaquine — Adverse Effects

Haemolysis in G6PD deficiency (screen before giving!); methaemoglobinaemia; abdominal cramps; nausea; headache; pruritus. Contraindicated in pregnancy (haemolysis in G6PD-deficient fetus).

Clinical Pearl

Always check G6PD before primaquine — haemolysis in G6PD deficiency can be fatal. Primaquine is essential for P. vivax radical cure — kills hypnozoites (dormant liver forms) that cause relapse; without primaquine, P. vivax relapses in 20-60% within months. 14-day course is standard (some use 7 days in SE Asia; 14 days in India). Tafenoquine — single-dose 8-aminoquinoline (300 mg) — radical cure in one dose; also requires G6PD screening; FDA-approved 2018. India — P. vivax accounts for ~50% of malaria cases; chloroquine still effective in most areas; chloroquine-resistant in northeast (use ACT). India NTEP/NVBDCP: free diagnosis (RDT/microscopy) & treatment; ASHA workers for community-level management.
q2_1_0_5:
Drugs for Diabetes Mellitus

Classification

Insulin: Rapid-acting (lispro, aspart, glulisine); Short-acting (regular); Intermediate (NPH/isophane); Long-acting (glargine, detemir, degludec); Premixed.

Oral hypoglycemic agents (OHAs):

  • Biguanides: Metformin — ↓ hepatic gluconeogenesis; ↑ insulin sensitivity; first-line for T2DM.
  • Sulfonylureas: Glimepiride, Gliclazide, Glipizide, Glibenclamide — ↑ insulin secretion (close KATP channel on beta cell).
  • DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins): Sitagliptin, Vildagliptin, Linagliptin, Saxagliptin, Alogliptin — ↑ GLP-1 (incretin effect).
  • SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins): Dapagliflozin, Empagliflozin, Canagliflozin, Ertugliflozin — ↓ renal glucose reabsorption → glucosuria.
  • GLP-1 receptor agonists: Exenatide, Liraglutide, Dulaglutide, Semaglutide, Tirzepatide (GIP/GLP-1 dual) — ↑ insulin, ↓ glucagon, ↓ gastric emptying, ↓ appetite.
  • Thiazolidinediones (glitazones): Pioglitazone, Rosiglitizone — ↑ insulin sensitivity (PPAR-gamma).
  • Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors: Acarbose, Miglitol, Voglibose — ↓ carbohydrate digestion/absorption.
  • Meglitinides (glinides): Repaglinide, Nateglinide — ↑ insulin secretion (short-acting).
  • Bile acid sequestrants: Colesevelam — ↓ bile acid reabsorption; modest glucose lowering.
  • Dopamine D2 agonist: Bromocriptine QR — ↓ hepatic gluconeogenesis.

Mechanism of Metformin

Activates AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) → ↓ hepatic gluconeogenesis (main effect); ↑ insulin sensitivity in muscle (↑ glucose uptake); ↓ intestinal glucose absorption; ↓ fatty acid oxidation; does NOT stimulate insulin secretion → no hypoglycaemia; no weight gain (may cause weight loss).

Adverse Effects of Metformin

GI (nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal discomfort — dose-related, start low, take with food, extended-release formulation); vitamin B12 deficiency (long-term — ↓ absorption); lactic acidosis (rare but fatal — accumulate in renal failure; contraindicated if eGFR <30; hold before contrast, surgery, severe illness); metallic taste.

Therapeutic Uses of Metformin

T2DM first-line (all patients unless contraindicated); pre-diabetes (IFG/IGT — high-risk); PCOS (insulin resistance); non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD); weight management (adjunct).

Contraindications of Metformin

eGFR <30 mL/min; acute kidney injury; severe hepatic disease; acute heart failure; hypoxia/shock/sepsis; before IV contrast (hold 48h); alcoholism; pregnancy (historically — now used in GDM if needed; insulin preferred).

Clinical Pearl

Metformin is first-line for all T2DM (unless contraindicated) — reduces CV events, mortality (UKPDS trial); no hypoglycaemia; weight neutral/loss; cheap. SGLT2 inhibitors — revolutionary — reduce HF hospitalisation, CV mortality (EMPA-REG, CANVAS), slow CKD progression (DAPA-CKD); now first-line add-on for T2DM with HF/CKD. GLP-1 agonists — reduce CV events, weight loss (5-15%); semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly approved for obesity (Wegovy). Tirzepatide (dual GIP/GLP-1) — most effective (HbA1c ↓2-3%, weight loss 15-20%). Insulin — T1DM (essential); T2DM when OHAs fail or severe hyperglycaemia. India — diabetes capital (~77 million); metformin widely available & cheap; SGLT2 & GLP-1 increasingly used but cost barrier; lifestyle modification essential.
q2_1_0_6:
Oral Hypoglycemic Agents — Sulfonylureas

Classification

First-generation (rarely used): Tolbutamide, Chlorpropamide, Glibenclamide (glyburide). Second-generation: Glipizide, Gliclazide, Glimepiride (most commonly used).

Mechanism of Action

Bind to SUR1 subunit of KATP channel on pancreatic beta-cell membrane → close KATP channel → membrane depolarisation → opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channel → Ca2+ influx → insulin granule exocytosis → ↑ insulin secretion. Requires functioning beta cells (ineffective in T1DM).

Pharmacokinetics

Oral; well absorbed; hepatic metabolism; renal excretion (glibenclamide has active metabolites — caution in CKD); glimepiride — longest duration (24h, once daily); gliclazide — modified release once daily.

Therapeutic Uses

T2DM — second-line after metformin (if metformin contraindicated or inadequate); especially if insulin deficiency predominant (lean T2DM); cheap; rapid onset.

Adverse Effects

Hypoglycaemia — most common & most important; especially in elderly, renal impairment, irregular meals, alcohol; glibenclamide highest risk (avoid in elderly & CKD); glimepiride lower risk. Weight gain — 1-2 kg (insulinotropic effect). Hyponatraemia (SIADH — especially chlorpropamide). Cardiovascular safety — controversial (older concerns about KATP channel blockade in heart; UGDP trial — tolbutamide ↑ CV mortality; modern evidence — glimepiride neutral). Photosensitivity, rash. Hepatotoxicity (rare). Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (chlorpropamide).

Contraindications

T1DM; diabetic ketoacidosis; pregnancy (crosses placenta — neonatal hypoglycaemia; use insulin); severe renal/hepatic impairment; sulfa allergy (cross-reactivity — low but caution); elderly (hypoglycaemia risk — avoid glibenclamide).

Drug Interactions

↑ Effect (hypoglycaemia): NSAIDs, sulfonamides, warfarin, fluconazole, miconazole, clarithromycin, cimetidine, alcohol, MAOIs, beta-blockers (also mask hypoglycaemia symptoms). ↓ Effect (hyperglycaemia): corticosteroids, thiazides, phenytoin, sympathomimetics, OCPs, niacin.

Clinical Pearl

Hypoglycaemia is the most important adverse effect — especially in elderly, CKD, irregular meals; always educate patient about symptoms & carry glucose. Glibenclamide (glyburide) has highest hypoglycaemia risk — avoid in elderly & CKD; use glimepiride (lower risk, once daily) or gliclazide MR instead. Second-line after metformin — if insulin deficiency predominant; cheap; rapid onset. Masking of hypoglycaemia by beta-blockers — tremor, palpitations masked (except sweating); educate diabetic patients. India — sulfonylureas widely used & cheap; glimepiride most common; often combined with metformin (FDC). Newer drugs (SGLT2, GLP-1) preferred for patients with CV/CKD/HF.
